narrative:
The model predicts you have a 24% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your lack of desire to pursue higher education, your history of past class failures, and your reason for choosing this school. Wanting to continue studying after high school is the single most important factor. Every student who passed expressed a clear wish to pursue higher education, while you do not. This absence of that goal pulled the prediction strongly toward failing. Your record of one previous failure also pushed the outcome toward failure; students who passed had zero past failures on average. Finally, choosing the school because it was close to home worked in the opposite direction, slightly increasing the chance you would pass, but this positive influence was not enough to outweigh the other two factors.

To improve, you should first reflect on whether your goals have changed and if you can find motivation to aim higher. Reducing future absences, which are already much higher than the average of under four days among students who passed, and increasing your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend would also help build a stronger foundation. Taking these steps now, while you still have the support of remedial classes, gives you the best chance to turn things around.
